newsitem.title: USA: Labor secretary offers little solace in Pabst case.
newsitem.headline: Labor secretary offers little solace in Pabst case.

text.p: Labor Secretary Robert Reich on Wednesday backed legislation that would curb the degree to which companies can cut off benefits to retirees but offered little solace to nearly 800 retired brewery workers already facing the prospect.
Reich told a group of Pabst Brewing Co. retirees that the country's sixth largest brewer acted "in my view illegally" when it terminated medical and death benefits to its retirees.

Reich said the Labor Department had filed a friend-of-the-court brief in the case and would back legislation, introduced by Milwaukee-area House members, to limit practices such as occurred in the Pabst case.

"It won't mend everybody sitting in this room but it will help make sure in the future promises that companies make to their workers, pension promises, health promises, are kept," Reich told about 175 of the retirees attending a meeting.
Beyond that, he admitted, there is little more the government can do.

Pabst cut off the benefits after its contract with the Brewery Workers Union expired May 31. The union challenged the move but last month a federal judge refused to grant a permanent order preventing Pabst from carrying out the termination, clearing the way for it to happen.
The company, which still has no agreement with the union, said the move would save it $3.5 million a year. After the old pact expired it put a new wage scale in place.

Pabst, founded in 1884, has laid off about 300 workers in the last 18 months and has about 120 remaining on its work force. A recent industry report by PaineWeber said Pabst's share of the domestic beer market had fallen to 3.9 percent.
Pabst has complained of losing money for more than a year, in competition with microbreweries and the market leader, St. Louis-based Anheuser Busch Cos. Inc., the maker of Budweiser.
The workers, most of them drinking Miller beer, listened glumly to Reich.
"I hope they go bankrupt, I really do," said a 63-year-old woman. "I can't get insurance at my age. Now what am I going to do?"
